section_summary: The section concludes a lengthy report on Japanese Communist activity among youth, farmers, women, the press, theater groups, and students, followed by a list of organizations and a bibliography. Later documents examine the party’s headquarters, the prospect of a Communist popular front, university recruitment, election results, and conditions under the Occupation. The final memorandum begins a report about party organization in Hokkaido and continues beyond this section.

subfiles.title: Report on postwar Communist activities in Japan, with organizational list and bibliography
subfiles.about: Surveys Communist organizing and influence across Japanese society and concludes with an organizational index and source bibliography.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion assesses Communist efforts among youth, farmers, women, newspapers, theater groups, teachers, and students. It argues that front organizations, propaganda, and control of key posts can extend party influence beyond membership numbers. Its conclusion considers historical, economic, and regional conditions favorable to Communism; the final pages list organizations by degree of influence and cite supporting reports.

subfiles.title: Headquarters of the Japan Communist Party
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits and evaluates a translated magazine article about the Communist Party’s Tokyo headquarters.
subfiles.summary: The adviser considers the article’s description of low wages, strict discipline, and member discontent broadly supported, but disputes its claim that the party is rich. The despatch identifies several people mentioned in the article and notes that party membership had also grown.

subfiles.title: Inside Japan Communist Party Headquarters
subfiles.from: Sempu; translated by Rengo News Service
subfiles.about: Describes the party’s Yoyogi headquarters, employees, finances, leadership, and research network.
subfiles.summary: The article depicts a cluster of party offices and affiliated businesses near the Yoyogi headquarters. It alleges low wages, long hours, unequal treatment, factional favoritism, and mounting internal discontent. It also provides claims about fundraising, publication circulation, black-market activity, and the personnel of the party’s Research Division.

subfiles.title: Telegram concerning a possible Communist popular front in Japan
subfiles.to: Acting Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Requests discussion with General MacArthur of reports that Japanese Communists may form a popular front.
subfiles.summary: The Department warns that a popular front could permit Communist infiltration and eventual domination of non-Communist allies. It urges discreet support for Japanese efforts to keep Communists politically isolated and asks the adviser to discuss the issue with MacArthur.

subfiles.title: Cover memorandum for popular-front telegram
subfiles.about: Forwards the draft telegram to the Acting Political Adviser in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Butterworth sends Lovett the telegram for review before transmission.

subfiles.title: MacArthur’s views on the Communist threat and popular front
subfiles.about: Reports MacArthur’s response to the Department’s concerns about a Communist popular front.
subfiles.summary: MacArthur describes the party’s immediate political threat as limited, although he sees Communist control of strategic labor unions as a serious danger. He considers a broad popular front unlikely and suggests a left-wing Social Democratic split could strengthen the remainder of that party. He also argues that criticism from Washington and perceived inequities in Occupation policy aid Communist propaganda.

subfiles.title: Letter commenting on MacArthur’s popular-front response
subfiles.about: Disagrees privately with MacArthur’s assessment of the Communist threat and its political implications.
subfiles.summary: The writer says the mission sees a greater Communist threat and fears obstacles to Yoshida’s government could benefit the left.

subfiles.title: Transmission of material on Communist united-front tactics
subfiles.to: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Sends background material for discussions and efforts concerning a Communist united front in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwards two documents on united-front tactics for the adviser’s use.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese affairs and the spread of Communism
subfiles.about: Summarizes observations on university Communism, a possible popular front, living standards, and Occupation policy.
subfiles.summary: The writer attributes growing Communist interest in universities to economic hardship, political scandal, international developments, and effective organization. He urges attention to a possible popular front and argues that improved living conditions are essential. He recommends transferring more responsibility to Japanese authorities and reducing the Occupation’s detailed control.

subfiles.title: Change in Japan Communist Party’s campaign strategy
subfiles.about: Describes the party’s appeal to small businesses during the election campaign.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum highlights tax advice, criticism of government taxes, and labor-management cooperation as efforts to broaden Communist support.

subfiles.title: Initial comment on Japanese election returns of January 23
subfiles.about: Assesses Yoshida’s majority and the Communist Party’s gains in the January election.
subfiles.summary: Bishop sees Yoshida’s majority as a possible sign of greater Japanese political responsibility, while noting the difficulty of governing under Occupation authority. He regards Communist electoral gains as evidence of wider influence and warns that the party may press labor and socialist groups toward a common front.

subfiles.title: Communist Party of Japan
subfiles.about: Relays a Hawaii Times article alleging stronger Communist organization in Hokkaido.
subfiles.summary: The quoted article names Shintoku, Sunagawa, and Obihiro branches and discusses a possible headquarters move to Hokkaido.
